Unreal
un-REEL
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
From English un- (not) and real, from Latin realis (actual, belonging to things). In 1828 unreal meant simply not real, unsubstantial. The slang sense — so good it is hard to believe, amazing ("That car is unreal!") — is American and belongs to the mid-twentieth century; it was in the mouths of 1950s teenagers and has never quite left. The word praises a thing by saying it seems too good to exist.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A teenager in 1958, looking at a new Corvette or the first color television on the block, would say "That’s unreal!" — meaning it was so good it hardly seemed possible. The Christian smiles at that, because the gospel is the one thing in the world that sounds unreal and is the realest thing there is. When the women came from the empty tomb and told the apostles that Jesus was alive, "their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not" (Luk 24:11). Even when the risen Lord stood before them, "they yet believed not for joy, and wondered" (Luk 24:41) — it was too good to be true, and it was true. That is the pattern of God’s works: "it is marvellous in our eyes" (Psa 118:23). The things God has prepared for His people are beyond anything a teenager could dream: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1Co 2:9). Paul says the unseen things are the lasting ones: "the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal" (2Co 4:18). The Corvette rusts. The resurrection stands. A grandfather can tell his grandchildren: when something seems unreal, give thanks — and save your loudest "unreal" for the empty tomb.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (1950s) for amazing, too good to believe — turning the 1828 sense of not real on its head, and a reminder that the resurrection seemed unreal to the apostles and was the realest thing of all (Luk 24:41).

expand to see more

UNREAL, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Amazing; beyond belief; wonderful. "Did you see that catch? Unreal!"

Webster (1828) — UNREAL, adjective not real; not substantial; having appearance only.

Decode for families: "unreal" is praise, not doubt — it means "so good I can hardly believe it."

Key Scripture

Luk 24:11 — "And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not."

Luk 24:41 — "And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered, he said unto them, Have ye here any meat?"

Psa 118:23 — "This is the LORD'S doing; it is marvellous in our eyes."

1Co 2:9 — "But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him."

2Co 4:18 — "While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal."

Modern Corruption

A harmless word of wonder; its only weakness is that it spends its amazement on cars and ballgames, and it can teach us to call the most real things the least believable.

expand to see more

Unreal is exaggeration of the friendly kind, the same family as far-out and awesome. No one who said it meant to deny anything; they meant to praise. There is nothing to correct in it.

There is something to notice, though. A generation that says "unreal" of a new car may come to feel that the spiritual world is the unreal one — that heaven, the resurrection, and the judgment are pious tales. Scripture turns that around (2Co 4:18). The seen is passing; the unseen is solid. A Christian can use the slang freely and still teach that the most amazing things God has done are not unreal at all.

Latin realis (actual) → English real → unreal (not real, 1828) → 1950s slang (amazing, too good to be true).
